title: Architecture scrub - dedicated vs hosted (KV / batching / quant)
summary: Deep technical session comparing Redwood Dedicated and Hosted architectures focused on throughput guarantees, noisy-neighbor mitigation, KV cache behavior, dynamic batching, and quantization tradeoffs. Customer is evaluating Dedicated for a regulated near-real-time product but is sensitive to cost. Action items include running targeted benchmarks and sharing security artifacts.
topics: KV cache hot-spot behavior and eviction
transcript:
[00:00:00] Lena (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:00:06] Priya Shah: Priya here. Sorry I'm joining from a noisy place.
[00:00:09] Tom Beck: Tom, platform.
[00:00:11] Jordan Li: Jordan, security.
[00:00:13] Marco (SE): Marco Ruiz, infra/serving.
[00:00:16] Lena: Cool. We put together an architecture scrub to walk through dedicated vs hosted, and dig into KV cache/batching/quantization since those are the big cost and latency levers. Priya, quick refresher on what success looks like for Alder?
[00:00:31] Priya: Two things mainly - first, latency p99 under 120ms for short generation calls (prompt+50 tokens) in primary region; second, predictable throughput for peak windows, around 800 concurrent low-latency requests. Also need strong audit logs and KMS integration for customer data.
[00:00:49] Lena: Ok got it. That maps to what we usually see. Marco, do you want to start on isolation differences?
[00:00:53] Marco: Sure — so high level: Hosted is multi-tenant with per-request routing and soft isolation via quotas and priority. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools per tenant and stronger isolation for noisy-neighbor protection. Practically that means Dedicated can enforce capacity guarantees — you get a reserved slot count and can shape burst policies. Hosted is cheaper for low steady load, but you can hit tail-latency spikes during cluster load.
[00:01:19] Tom: Can you quantify "tail spikes"? Like p99 degradation in multi-tenant?
[00:01:23] Marco: It varies by model and traffic shape but we've seen p99 jump from 90ms to 220ms during noisy periods on shared pools for small-generation patterns. Those numbers are our public averages, but again dependent on sequence lengths and KV cache hit rates. With Dedicated the p99 typically stays within your SLO +/- 10-20ms because the runtime can allocate fewer contexts per GPU and we can tune batch windows.
[00:01:43] Jordan: On the security side, can Dedicated run in our VPC with customer-managed KMS?
[00:01:47] Marco: Yes - Dedicated + Private offers VPC peering or private connectivity and customer-managed KMS/HSM. Hosted currently only supports envelope encryption and Redwood-managed KMS, though we provide enterprise key custody options in some regions. We'll share the SOC2 and KMS docs after.
[00:02:02] Lena: Note to send security pack (see action items).
[00:02:04] Priya: Cool. Let's talk KV cache — we rely heavily on prefix caching for chat continuity and to avoid recomputation. How deterministic are cache hit rates across workloads?
[00:02:13] Marco: Good question. Cache hit rate depends on prompt similarity and how you structure prompts. For many customers with high reuse patterns we see 40-70% token-level hit rate with prefix caching. Two important failure modes: hot-key pressure (a few sessions monopolize KV) and cold-start churn after deployments. With Dedicated we can allocate larger cached segments per tenant and tune eviction (LRU vs LFU). Hosted uses a shared cache tier where eviction is more aggressive.
[00:02:42] Tom: If a hot key causes evictions, what's the impact on latency?
[00:02:46] Marco: If a relevant entry is evicted, that request will recompute tokens and may add ~30-80ms depending on model size. For long-sequence workloads, the recompute can be higher. We recommend configuring segmentation for conversational usage and using sticky sessions in Dedicated to increase locality.
[00:03:03] Priya: Sticky sessions — is that something you'd run client-side or within the routing layer?
[00:03:07] Marco: We offer routing affinity at the load balancer layer for Dedicated and can provide SDK hints. For Hosted, affinity is soft but available via a session token header — can't be guaranteed under cluster rebalancing.
[00:03:19] Lena: Let's pivot to batching: dynamic batching vs fixed windows. Marco?
[00:03:23] Marco: Redwood runtime supports continuous batching: the system collects tokens across inflight requests and issues kernels once thresholds (time or count) hit. For low-latency requirements we tune the time cap (e.g., 10-15ms) to avoid waiting for large batches. This reduces cost but increases tail latency if not tuned. Dedicated allows you to set tighter batching policies per tenant so you can favor latency over throughput.
[00:03:45] Tom: So on Dedicated I can set batch max latency to like 8ms? Would that still get reasonable GPU utilization?
[00:03:50] Marco: It depends on QPS. If you have steady QPS, even small batch windows can achieve good utilization. If your traffic is very spiky with bursts, you may lose efficiency; Dedicated's reserved pool helps there since you won't be competing with other tenants. We can also combine with microburst burst capacity to soak transient peaks.
[00:04:07] Priya: Quantization — we plan to try int8 or int4 to reduce cost. Any caveats on quality or KV interactions?
[00:04:12] Marco: Quantization is great for throughput/cost. Int8 typically preserves almost identical quality for most models; int4 sometimes has subtle regressions that show up in edge-case prompts. For KV cache, quantization doesn't affect cache semantics, but it does change per-token compute time and memory footprint which affects how many sessions you can hold in GPU memory. We recommend a two-stage: run int8 in prod, and try int4 on a canary subset with quality evals.
[00:04:35] Jordan: Do you support mixed-precision kernels and fallback to FP16 for critical queries?
[00:04:38] Marco: Yes. The runtime supports mixed kernels and can route specific model variants or tenants to FP16/FP32 backends on demand. Fallback policies can be automatic based on anomaly detection (e.g., quality regression) or explicit routing rules.
[00:04:50] Tom: How about deterministic rollouts? We need A/B compare outputs for quality checks during quant rollout.
[00:04:55] Marco: Redwood Console supports rollouts — you can split traffic by percentage and collect side-by-side eval metrics. We'll keep KVs separate per variant to avoid cross-contamination.
[00:05:05] Priya: Benchmarks — can you run 99th percentile tests that mimic our traffic? We have spiky daily reports with sudden bursts.
[00:05:11] Lena: That's in the action items. Marco will run a synthetic 48-hour test with our supplied trace.
[00:05:15] Marco: Yep, we'll ingest Tom's trace and run both Dedicated reservation and Hosted sim to show p50/p95/p99, cost delta, and KV hit behavior. Expect artifacts in about a week.
[00:05:24] Tom: For Dedicated pricing, curious about how we size the GPU pool. If we ask for 20 reserved workers, how do you translate to throughput?
[00:05:30] Marco: We'll supply a capacity planner sheet. Rough estimate: with smaller models (e.g., 7B-like), one GPU worker might handle ~1500-2500 tokens/sec under mixed batching; big models drop that significantly. We'll include token-level throughput and effective requests/sec assuming your average tokens per request.
[00:05:44] Jordan: Audit logs — can we get per-token tracing for debug, and how long are they retained?
[00:05:48] Lena: We have token-level traces but need to check retention windows for Dedicated vs Hosted. For enterprise we can extend retention in Dedicated as an add-on.
[00:05:56] Jordan: Must be encrypted at rest with our KMS.
[00:05:58] Marco: Supported in Dedicated private. We'll add a doc link.
[00:06:02] [00:20:10] Priya: A question on evictions — when you evict KV, is there a soft-miss amplification where you have to refetch other context?
[00:20:16] Marco: If evictions are coarse-grained (e.g., shard eviction) you can get adjacent misses. We advise smaller shard sizes for conversational workloads to limit blast radius. Dedicated allows you to specify shard sizing and give you metrics on per-shard hit rates.
[00:20:33] Tom: If we go Dedicated, can we bring our own nodes on-prem later?
[00:20:38] Lena: Yes — Redwood Private supports on-prem deployments with the same control plane; that path is common for regulated customers in phase 2.
[00:20:44] Priya: Anything to call out about dev iteration speed? On Hosted we can iterate faster, right?
[00:20:48] Marco: Correct, Hosted is quicker for spinning up experiments. Dedicated has more provisioning lead time but we provide dev tiers and ephemeral pools for dev/test. Real customers often use Hosted for early experimentation and Dedicated once they hit production SLOs.
[00:21:00] Jordan: On compliance, do you support SAML SSO + SCIM?
[00:21:04] Lena: Yes, enterprise features include SAML/SCIM and RBAC. We'll attach the setup guide.
[00:21:08] Tom: Are there any gotchas with cross-region KG cache consistency? Our users are global but we prefer sticky region routing.
[00:21:14] Marco: Cross-region is tricky: KV caches are regional. You can route users to region-affinity to keep locality. For global users you'll see lower hit rates unless you pre-warm or replicate hot entries. Replication costs increase with state size.
[00:21:29] Priya: Ok makes sense.
[00:21:31] Marco: Quick note on tail-latency strategies: 1) pre-warm inference contexts during expected peaks; 2) use small fixed batch windows for short-response SLAs; 3) maintain a warm reserve in Dedicated; 4) use model variants for cheap fast-fallback (smaller quantized model) for latency-critical requests.
[00:21:51] Priya: For fallbacks, will the response quality difference be obvious?
[00:21:54] Marco: It depends on prompt. For many prompts smaller quantized models are acceptable; Console rollout/Bias tests will help quantify.
[00:21:59] Lena: Okay, let's cover next steps and owners.
[00:22:03] Lena: Marco to run bench with provided trace, share graphs (p50/p95/p99), KV hit heatmaps, and cost comparison (Hosted vs Dedicated) — due 2025-12-07.
[00:22:13] Marco: Yep.
[00:22:14] Lena: Lena to share SOC2/KMS/SAML docs and Dedicated sizing worksheet — due 2025-12-03.
[00:22:20] Lena: Tom to share representative traffic trace and evaluation prompts — due 2025-12-01.
[00:22:25] Tom: Will do.
[00:22:27] Lena: Priya to pick 10 core prompts for int4 canary and define quality thresholds — due 2025-12-04.
[00:22:33] Priya: I'll get that to you.
[00:22:35] Jordan: We'll need a security review slot after benchmark results.
[00:22:38] Lena: Noted, we'll schedule.
[00:22:40] [00:56:30] Tom: One last quick: if Dedicated shows 15% higher baseline cost but gives consistent p99, what's typical negotiation on committed term?
[00:56:39] Lena: We can do committed reserved discounts, annual pricing tiers, and include extra observability retention as part of the deal. More specifics after the bench results.
[00:56:47] Priya: Thanks — super helpful.
[00:56:49] Marco: Thanks everyone.
[00:56:51] Lena: We'll follow up with artifacts and next meeting invite.
